attempt-where-did-i-go-wrong.response:
Your setup was right — using $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)$ and letting the pulse set the limits is exactly the way to go. Two things break between that line and $te^{-t}$.

**First genuine error: the integrand.** You replaced $h(t-\tau)$ with $e^{-t}$, which drops the $\tau$ dependence:

$$h(t-\tau) = e^{-(t-\tau)}u(t-\tau), \qquad x(\tau)=u(\tau)-u(\tau-1)=\begin{cases}1,&0<\tau<1\\0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

Keeping your own limits, $\int_0^t e^{-(t-\tau)}\,d\tau = t\left(1-e^{-t}\right)$, not $te^{-t}$. Pulling $e^{-t}$ out of the integral is only legal when nothing else in the integrand depends on $\tau$ — here $e^{\tau}$ was discarded along with it.

**Second error: the upper limit.** $u(t-\tau)$ requires $\tau<t$, so the upper limit is $t$ *only while the pulse is still open*. Since $x(\tau)$ vanishes for $\tau>1$, the limit saturates at $1$. The correct single expression is

$$y(t)=\int_{0}^{\min(t,\,1)} e^{-(t-\tau)}\,d\tau,\qquad t>0$$

with $y(t)=0$ for $t<0$ (no overlap: the pulse lives on $[0,1]$, the shifted kernel on $\tau<t$).

Evaluating the two regimes:

$$y(t)=\begin{cases}0, & t<0\\[4pt] 1-e^{-t}, & 0\le t<1\\[4pt] (e-1)\,e^{-t}, & t\ge 1\end{cases}$$

Sanity checks I ran: at $t=1$ both branches give $1-e^{-1}=(e-1)e^{-1}\approx0.632$, so $y$ is continuous; $y(0.5)=1-e^{-0.5}\approx0.393$; and for $t>1$ the response is just the tail of the kernel carrying the fixed area $\int_0^1 e^{\tau}d\tau=e-1$ scaled by $e^{-t}$. Physically: the output ramps up while the pulse is feeding the system, then decays at the system's own rate once the input turns off.

vector-space-definition.response:
A vector space is a set of objects — vectors — that you're allowed to add together and stretch by numbers (scalars), in a way that behaves like the arrows you've seen in geometry. Concretely, you need a set $V$, a field of scalars like $\mathbb{R}$, an addition that takes any two elements of $V$ back into $V$, and a scalar multiplication that also lands back in $V$; on top of that, the operations have to obey the familiar rules — you can regroup and reorder sums, there's a zero vector that does nothing, every vector has a negative that cancels it, and scaling distributes over both vector addition and scalar addition. The key idea is that the "vectors" don't have to be arrows at all: anything is a vector space as long as those two operations exist and play by those rules, which is why the same theorems apply to matrices, functions, and solutions of a differential equation all at once.

Small example: $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the usual componentwise addition $(a,b)+(c,d)=(a+c,b+d)$ and scaling $k(a,b)=(ka,kb)$ is a vector space; the same recipe makes $\mathbb{R}^n$ one, and polynomials of degree at most 2 form one too, where "adding vectors" is just adding polynomials.

vector-space-start-heldout.response:
Start with **closure under addition**, because that's the only place the "degree at most 2" restriction could actually bite — everything else (associativity, distributivity, additive inverses) is inherited from the surrounding space of all polynomials once you know the set is closed and contains the zero polynomial.

Write two completely general elements, with unrelated coefficients rather than specific polynomials:

$$p(t) = a_2 t^2 + a_1 t + a_0, \qquad q(t) = b_2 t^2 + b_1 t + b_1 t + b_0, \qquad a_i, b_i \in \mathbb{R}$$

then form $p(t) + q(t)$ and ask a single question of the result: *can the coefficient of any power of $t$ exceed degree 2?* Watch what happens to the $t^2$ coefficient in the special case $a_2 = -b_2$, and ask yourself whether the outcome you get is still allowed by the words "at most 2" — that comparison is the whole test, and it's the reason this set behaves differently from the set of polynomials of degree **exactly** 2.

Give that a try, then do the same with $\alpha p(t)$ for $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$.
